items.q: Stack vs heap — what actually differs?
items.a_short: Stack: automatic lifetime, LIFO, fast pointer-bump allocation, small and fixed size. Heap: manual lifetime, slower allocator, large, fragments.
items.a_full: On an embedded target the stack is often only a few KB, so a large local array blows it with no MMU to catch the fault — it just corrupts adjacent memory. Many safety-critical embedded codebases forbid heap allocation entirely to make memory use statically provable.

options: Stack: automatic LIFO lifetime, fast, small. Heap: manual, slower, large, fragments
They are the same memory region

items.q: What does this print on a 64-bit machine?
items.a_short: `40` then `8` — the array decays to a pointer when passed to a function.
items.a_full: `sizeof(a)` in main is 10 × 4 bytes. Inside `f`, the parameter is really `int *arr`, so `sizeof` gives the pointer size. This is why C functions taking arrays must also take a length — there is no way to recover it.

items.q: Name the four classic C memory bugs.
items.a_short: Memory leak (never freed), dangling pointer / use-after-free, double free, and buffer overflow.
items.a_full: Set a pointer to NULL immediately after freeing — `free(NULL)` is a safe no-op, so this neutralizes double free and makes use-after-free crash loudly instead of corrupting silently. Tooling: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer, static analysers.

options: Leak, use-after-free, double free, buffer overflow

items.q: What is `sizeof(struct S)` on a typical 64-bit system, and why?
items.a_short: 12 bytes — 3 bytes of padding after `a` to align `b`, and 3 trailing bytes so the struct's size is a multiple of its alignment.
items.a_full: Reordering to `int b; char a; char c;` gives 8 bytes. Ordering members largest-first is free memory savings, which matters when you have arrays of millions of structs. Packing with `#pragma pack` removes padding but causes unaligned access, which is slow on ARM and a hard fault on some cores.

items.q: Why does loop order change matrix traversal speed so dramatically in C?
items.a_short: C is row-major. Iterating rows-then-columns walks contiguous memory and uses every byte of each cache line; the reverse order strides past memory and misses on nearly every access.
items.a_full: A 64-byte cache line holds 16 floats. Row-major order gets 16 useful values per miss; column-major order gets 1. The slowdown is commonly 5-10×, with identical FLOPs — a direct demonstration that memory access patterns, not arithmetic, decide real performance.

options: C is row-major; row-order traversal uses full cache lines, column-order wastes them

items.q: What does `volatile` mean and when is it required?
items.a_short: It tells the compiler the value can change outside the program's control, so it must re-read it from memory and not optimize accesses away.
items.a_full: Required for memory-mapped hardware registers, variables modified by an ISR, and variables touched by `setjmp`/`longjmp`. It is *not* a concurrency primitive — it guarantees nothing about atomicity or memory ordering between threads. Use `_Atomic` or proper synchronization for that.

options: It forces re-reads from memory for values that change outside program control

items.q: What does this print, and why is it surprising?
items.a_short: `not less` — the usual arithmetic conversions promote `i` to unsigned, turning −1 into 4294967295.
items.a_full: This is a real source of security bugs: a signed length check against an unsigned size passes when it shouldn't. Compile with `-Wsign-compare` and keep size types consistent (`size_t` throughout).

items.q: What's the difference between `const int *p`, `int *const p` and `const int *const p`?
items.a_short: Pointer to const int (can't change the value), const pointer to int (can't repoint it), and const pointer to const int (neither).
items.a_full: Read declarations right to left from the identifier: `int * const p` → 'p is a const pointer to int'. The `const int *` form is what you want for a read-only function parameter — it documents intent and lets the compiler catch accidental writes.

options: const int *p: value is const; int *const p: pointer is const; both const: neither changes
Only the third is valid C

items.q: What does `static` mean in C — all three contexts?
items.a_short: On a global or function: internal linkage, visible only in that translation unit. On a local variable: persistent storage, initialized once, retains its value across calls.
items.a_full: `static` on file-scope functions is the C equivalent of 'private' and lets the compiler inline more aggressively. A `static` local is stored in the data segment, not on the stack — which also makes it not thread-safe without synchronization.

options: Internal linkage at file scope; persistent single-initialized storage for locals

items.q: What is endianness and when does it bite you?
items.a_short: The byte order of multi-byte values. Little-endian stores the least significant byte first; big-endian the opposite. It matters for network protocols, file formats and binary blobs crossing machines.
items.a_full: x86 and ARM (in practice) are little-endian; network byte order is big-endian, hence `htons`/`ntohl`. Never `memcpy` a struct across a wire or into a file and read it back on another architecture — serialize field by field with an explicit byte order.

options: Byte order of multi-byte values; matters for networks, files and cross-machine binary data

items.q: Set, clear, toggle and test bit n of a register.
items.a_short: Set `r |= (1u << n)`, clear `r &= ~(1u << n)`, toggle `r ^= (1u << n)`, test `(r >> n) & 1u`.
items.a_code:
#define BIT(n)        (1u << (n))
#define SET(r, n)     ((r) |=  BIT(n))
#define CLR(r, n)     ((r) &= ~BIT(n))
#define TOG(r, n)     ((r) ^=  BIT(n))
#define TST(r, n)     (((r) >> (n)) & 1u)
items.a_full: Use unsigned literals — `1 << 31` on a signed int is undefined behaviour. For hardware registers, the variable must also be `volatile`, and read-modify-write on a register an ISR also touches needs the interrupt disabled around it.

options: Set with |=, clear with &= ~, toggle with ^=

items.q: Why use fixed-point instead of floating-point on an MCU or DSP?
items.a_short: Many MCUs have no FPU, so float operations are emulated in software — 10-100× slower and larger code. Fixed-point uses the integer ALU.
items.a_full: Fixed-point also has uniform absolute precision across its range, which suits sensor data with a known scale, whereas float has uniform relative precision. The cost is that you manage the scaling yourself and must watch for overflow — there's no graceful degradation, values just wrap.

options: Many MCUs lack an FPU, so floats are emulated in software and far slower
Floating point uses more memory per value always
Fixed-point has a larger dynamic range

items.a_short: It returns a pointer to a stack array that is destroyed when the function returns — a dangling pointer.
items.a_full: The memory is reused by the next call, so the data looks fine immediately after and corrupts later, which makes it brutal to debug. Fixes: `malloc` the buffer (caller frees), take a caller-provided buffer and size, or use a `static` buffer if you accept the thread-safety cost.

options: Returns a pointer to a stack array that no longer exists

items.a_short: Two threads writing to different variables that happen to sit on the same cache line, forcing the line to ping-pong between cores.
items.a_full: Nothing is logically shared, but the cache coherence protocol invalidates the whole 64-byte line on every write. The fix is padding or alignment so each thread's data occupies its own line — `alignas(64)` on the struct, or padding fields. It shows up as a parallel program that gets slower with more threads.

options: Two threads reading the same variable
Threads writing different variables on the same cache line, causing coherence traffic
A race condition on a lock

items.q: What are the four stages from .c to executable?
items.a_short: Preprocess (expand macros and includes) → compile (to assembly) → assemble (to object code) → link (resolve symbols into an executable).
items.a_full: Knowing the stages makes errors readable: 'undefined reference' is a linker error (the symbol was declared but never defined, or you forgot `-l`), while 'implicit declaration' is a compiler error from a missing header. `gcc -E`, `-S`, `-c` stop after each stage.

items.q: What is SIMD and why does it matter for inference kernels?
items.a_short: Single Instruction, Multiple Data — one instruction operating on a vector of values. ARM NEON processes 16 INT8 lanes at once.
items.a_full: This is where INT8's speedup actually comes from: the same 128-bit register holds 4 FP32 values or 16 INT8 values, so the throughput ratio is 4×. Getting it requires contiguous, aligned data and no loop-carried dependencies — which is why data layout (NHWC vs NCHW) is a performance decision, not a formatting one.

options: One instruction operating on a vector of values — 16 INT8 lanes per 128-bit NEON register
